title: Beyond the three qualities
hookLine: He is beyond the three qualities that shape all things (Sukhmani 16)
tomorrow: Known by the one He blesses

cards: Monday morning, you're wired: fifteen tabs open, coffee half drunk, answering three people at once. Wednesday afternoon, you're heavy: you've read the same email four times and can't make yourself reply.

And once in a while, a Saturday walk where everything is clear and quiet and kind. Three moods, sometimes in one week, sometimes in one hour. It's easy to treat them as simply who we are: personality, sleep, coffee.
India's old philosophers gave those three a name, and the sixteenth ashtpadi uses it.

teach.h: GUNA: A STRAND OF THE ROPE.
teach.b: The salok says God is trihu gun te bhinn: beyond the three gunas. Gun, or guna, means quality, or strand, like the strands twisted together to make a rope.

In older Indian philosophy, everything in the world is woven from three such strands. Rajas: restless energy, drive, wanting, the Monday mood. Tamas: heaviness, dullness, inertia, the Wednesday afternoon.
And sattva: clarity, calm, balance, the Saturday walk. Every person, every day, every meal and mood is some mix of the three. Gurbani takes this picture up.

It speaks of maya, the world's pull, as made of three qualities, and it's honest about all three, even the nice one. You might expect calm sattva to be the goal. But the One is beyond all three, the calm included.

The three are weather. Good weather is lovely, but it still comes and goes. So Gurbani speaks of a fourth state, chautha pad, where a person rests in the One rather than in whatever mood is passing through.
That's surprisingly practical. If calm were the goal, every restless morning would be a failure.
If the goal is beyond all three, wired, heavy and clear are just strands passing by.
You can notice them without being them.
You can have a terrible Wednesday afternoon and still stand on something that isn't Wednesday afternoon.
The salok is describing God. It's also describing a place to stand.

how: Gurbani speaks of the three gunas and of a fourth state beyond them; Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's sixteenth salok hear that God is beyond all three.

o: the three Gurus who wrote Sukhmani Sahib
the three qualities woven through every mood
three fasts kept on set days each month

games.q: beyond the three qualities — tap the pairs.
p: the fourth state, beyond all three

s: in Gurbani, calm sattva is the final goal
the One is beyond all three; even calm is weather.
guna can mean a strand, as in the strands of a rope
everything is pictured as woven from three strands.
Gurbani speaks of a fourth state beyond the three qualities
chautha pad: resting in the One, not in a passing mood.

games.q: it's a heavy, dull afternoon and you can't focus. by the sixteenth ashtpadi, what's going on?
o: a strand of weather is passing; you can stand on something beyond it.
you need to force yourself into calm.
games.why: tamas is one of three strands, all weather. the salok places the One beyond all three, and Gurbani points to a fourth state beyond them.

practice: Ask yourself, without judging: is something restless in me right now, something heavy, something clear? Notice each one, without grabbing even the clear one.
Let all three pass like weather, and rest in whatever is noticing them; if you pray, rest in Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Trai gun, the three qualities. The One is beyond restless rajas, heavy tamas, and even calm sattva, and beyond all three.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: trai gun, the three qualities; the salok itself says trihu gun.

carryVoice: Your line: beyond the moods. Even calm is weather, and the One is beyond all three. That's day four hundred ninety-nine.
